extracted.intended_audience: physicians, masseurs/manipulators, nurses, and students of clinical manual therapy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical clinical guidance on when and how to apply massage (friction, kneading, percussion, pressure, movement) safely and effectively, plus required practitioner qualifications and training considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of massage
rubrics_metrics.description: Massage signifies a group of procedures usually done with the hands, such as friction, kneading, manipulating, rolling, and percussing of the external tissues of the body, used with curative, palliative, or hygienic objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include passive, resistive, or assistive movements (often called the Swedish movement-cure) within the term 'massage' where appropriate. Avoid confusing 'massage' with vague terms like 'rubbing' or overpromising with the word 'cure.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Indications and variable usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Massage may be of primary importance, secondary importance, of no use, or even injurious depending on the individual case and the stage of the disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply only where evidence or clinical judgment indicates benefit; recognize that in definite stages of many affections massage has proved directly or indirectly beneficial, but it is not universally appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner qualifications and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who would properly understand and apply massage should be familiar with its literature, the natural history of applicable maladies, the course of these affections when treated by usual methods, and the methods of other respectable practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such knowledge allows proper attribution of improvements or relapses and comparison of methods; lack of this knowledge undermines appropriate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required personal qualities and experience of the manipulator
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators should have abundance of time, patience, strength, and skill acquired by long and intelligent experience; they should be tender and gentle, yet strong and enduring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good masseurs are scarce; practical skill (the art) is required in addition to theoretical study. Avoid relying on those who lack endurance or the appropriate temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical constitution of practitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners of remarkable plethoric or fat appearance are often ill-suited to do massage; rather, operators should be rather thin but with sufficiently strong, muscular hands and firm tissues for endurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming external robustness implies aptitude for prolonged, confining manual work; choose operators with appropriate stamina and hand strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism and avoidance of quackery
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of individuals claiming mysterious powers, 'magnetism,' or facile cures; massage should be placed on its merits and practiced by educated physicians or properly trained persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training programs (e.g., for nurses) and instruction by competent physicians help bring massage within rational therapeutics; do not delegate to untrained persons who advertise 'massage' without skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: All massage procedures can be grouped under four heads: friction, percussion, pressure, and movement; malaxation, manipulation, deep-rubbing, kneading (proper massage) combine pressure and movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each procedure may be gentle, moderate, or vigorous depending on the case and operator; select modalities according to therapeutic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule for beginning and ending sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: All single or combined procedures should be begun moderately, gradually increased in force and frequency to the fullest desirable extent, and should end gradually as begun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid abrupt changes in intensity; progressive ramp-up and ramp-down protect comfort and circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use maximal palmar surface, not fingertips
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest extent of surface of the fingers and hands consistent with ease and efficacy of movement should be adapted to the surface worked upon so time is not lost by working with finger ends only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit the palmar surface into anatomical depressions for effective contact; use heel of hand for especially vigorous friction of the palm and sole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient positioning and environment
rubrics_metrics.description: The patient should be placed in as easy and comfortable a position as possible in a well-ventilated room at a temperature of about 70°F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comfortable positioning and appropriate ambient conditions support therapeutic effect and patient tolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dose determination
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes the dose of massage is determined by the force and frequency of manipulations and the length of time during which they are employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A skilled manipulator will accomplish more in a short time than an unskilled one in longer time; tailor dose to practitioner ability and patient tolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direction of rectilinear friction
rubrics_metrics.description: Rectilinear friction should always be used in an upward direction, from the extremities to the trunk, to favor and not retard the venous and lymphatic currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A light returning downward movement may be used to soothe without retarding circulation; think of the forward-and-return as the carpenter's plane analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid transverse (right-angle) friction
rubrics_metrics.description: Transverse friction at right angles to the long axis of a limb is an ungraceful, awkward procedure introduced on theoretical grounds and may with safety be laid aside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer rectilinear and circular friction which accomplish more than cross-wise rubbing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial segmentation and stroke length
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide extremities and trunk into convenient territories (e.g., fingers to wrist, wrist to elbow, elbow to shoulder; anterior/posterior/lateral aspects of legs) and make strokes of joint-to-joint length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic division avoids omission and ensures thorough coverage; adapt territories to body region size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended stroke rates by region
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested rapidities: double strokes 100–150/minute for fingers-to-wrist; oval circular friction 125–250 each hand (250–500 both hands); lower limb below knee 100–160 each hand; above knee 75–100 each; back and thighs about 60–75 each hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust rates for skin thickness, muscle mass, and patient size; larger areas warrant slower, longer strokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of circular (oval) friction
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful form of circular friction is oval-shaped with both hands moving so one ascends as the other descends, each at 125–250 strokes per minute (or combined counts as above).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply oval circular friction joint-to-joint, keeping upward stroke within limits of not chafing the skin; suitable for limbs and trunk where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Back and thigh technique considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: On back and thighs the skin is thicker and coarser and larger muscles can bear stronger pressure; strokes are longer and less rapid than on limbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect increased time expenditure and use stronger, longer strokes rather than high frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chest and abdominal directions and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Chest friction should be from insertion to origin of pectoral muscles; abdomen from right iliac fossa along ascending, transverse, and descending colon; friction is seldom necessary on abdomen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer other procedures (pressure/movement) for abdomen; avoid unnecessary friction on sensitive visceral areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity relative to tissue targeted
rubrics_metrics.description: Friction is intended primarily to act upon the skin; often the force used is much greater than necessary and there are better ways to affect deeper tissues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate redness or irritation with therapeutic benefit; tools (towel, brush) producing redness are not substitutes for skilled manual technique to reach deeper tissues safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust technique to case requirements and operator capability
rubrics_metrics.description: All procedures may be gentle, moderate, or vigorous according to the requirements of the case and the physical qualities of the operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select intensity, modality, stroke rate and duration based on patient condition, area treated, and operator endurance and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of method awareness and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should know the methods of others of respectable practice to compare them with their own and to adopt improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with contemporary methods (e.g., German, Scandinavian, French practices) aids in selecting appropriate techniques and avoiding empiricism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training cascade caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Passing limited, desultory instruction down in a cascade (one trained person teaches a few pupils who then teach others) often results in poor quality massage that retains only the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure systematic, thorough training and supervision rather than ad-hoc, diluted instruction to maintain standard of care.
